source.title: Basic IELTS Reading by Zhang Juan (Vietnamese edition, 2019)
source.publisher: Nhan Tri Viet / Beijing Language and Culture University Press
source.answerKeyOrigin: Checked against the supplied publisher Answer Key, book pages 169–173.
source.explanationOrigin: Written for WordHop and reviewed against the publisher key and the original reading text.

parts.title: Passage 1 · Help! Volunteers Wanted
parts.instructions: Follow the original instructions shown on the book pages. Choose the requested answer letters or True, False or Not Given.

questions.explanation: A volunteer offers services without being paid. Being willing to help alone does not give the full meaning.
questions.evidence: needs volunteers to help in her Tutorial Room

questions.explanation: Assigned means given or allocated a task. In this sentence, teachers give students interviews as homework. The publisher key selects B, given as a share or for use.
questions.evidence: assigned interviews for homework by their classroom teachers

questions.explanation: To relax is to rest, become less tense and stop worrying.
questions.evidence: relax in this comfortable environment

questions.explanation: An abridged book has been shortened while keeping the main content.
questions.evidence: helping students choose abridged books

questions.explanation: The publisher key confirms C, part that is less important. In ordinary usage, sub-part means a smaller section within a larger whole and does not necessarily compare importance. None of the printed choices states that precise meaning, so this item remains visible for review and is not scored.
questions.evidence: the Pronunciation Clinic, which is a sub-part of the Tutorial
questions.reviewNote: A sub-part is a subdivision, not necessarily a less important part. The printed options all compare importance.

questions.explanation: 'Intercultural' means involving or occurring between cultures.
questions.evidence: their understanding of intercultural differences

questions.explanation: The Tutorial Room is in the Wallace Lounge. The cafeteria and parking lot are landmarks used to describe its location.
questions.evidence: located at the Wallace Lounge

questions.explanation: It is offered on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays: three days each week.
questions.evidence: Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays

questions.explanation: The clinic is optional, and students may drop in for any length of time.
questions.evidence: if they wish, they can drop in for as long or as short as they want

questions.explanation: Seven students plus one volunteer make eight people, matching the eight-headphone station.
questions.evidence: an 8-headphone listening station ... a volunteer can work with up to 7 students

questions.explanation: Sherri is present specifically to help volunteers who have questions.
questions.evidence: Sherri is always in the Tutorial to help if a volunteer has any questions.

questions.explanation: Students are often given interview homework and come to ask volunteers for their opinions.
questions.evidence: go to the Tutorial to interview volunteers for their opinions

questions.explanation: The passage directly links the lounge's suitability for conversations to its large size and outside patio.
questions.evidence: ideal for conversations, as it is big and has an outside patio

questions.explanation: Students are encouraged to bring food and drinks themselves; the passage does not promise to supply them all.
questions.evidence: come with food or drinks

questions.explanation: A small lending library is mentioned, but the passage does not state where borrowed books may be taken or used. Taking them home cannot be established from the text. The publisher key is NOT GIVEN.
questions.evidence: Volunteers also help run the small lending library by helping students choose abridged books.

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly says students can borrow some tapes from the CALL Facility.
questions.evidence: borrow some of them from the CALL Facility

questions.explanation: Vocabulary games are available, but the passage does not say whether students enjoy playing them with volunteers.
questions.evidence: There are also vocabulary games such as Scrabble.

questions.explanation: Sherri ideally wants a regular commitment of at least one hour each week during the term.
questions.evidence: at least an hour a week on a regular basis for the term

questions.explanation: A full-term commitment is an ideal, not a requirement. People can help for part of the term or only occasionally.
questions.evidence: whether you are able to commit for part of the term, or just drop in once in a while

parts.title: Passage 2 · Modern Examinations
parts.instructions: Follow the original instructions shown on the book pages. Choose the requested answer letters or True, False or Not Given.

questions.explanation: To consist of something means be made up of it.
questions.evidence: testing usually consisted of saying poetry aloud or giving speeches

questions.explanation: 'Advanced' describes a high or far-developed level of study.
questions.evidence: working for advanced degrees

questions.explanation: A candidate is someone seeking a position or qualification; in the passage the candidates are being tested for a degree.
questions.evidence: testing candidates for the doctor's degree

questions.explanation: To resemble something is to look like it or be similar to it.
questions.evidence: resembles a group of workers at an automobile factory

questions.explanation: An objective judgement is based on facts rather than personal feelings or opinions.
questions.evidence: deal with facts, not personal opinions

questions.explanation: A broad question is general rather than focused on one particular detail.
questions.evidence: broad and general questions

questions.explanation: The passage names ancient Greece and Rome; Rome is the one included in the answer choices.
questions.evidence: In the schools of ancient Greece and Rome ... saying poetry aloud

questions.explanation: Rapid population growth is one possible explanation suggested for the arrival of written examinations.
questions.evidence: the great increase in population

questions.explanation: The writer explicitly compares the expected behaviour of teachers and students to machines.
questions.evidence: teachers and students are expected to act like machines

questions.explanation: Essay answers reduce the role of lucky guessing because students must produce their own explanations.
questions.evidence: it reduces the element of luck

questions.explanation: The final paragraph describes examinations as unsatisfactory. It does not say most teachers and students are satisfied with essay tests.
questions.evidence: Most teachers and students would probably agree that examinations are unsatisfactory.

questions.explanation: The second paragraph places discussions with subject specialists in European universities during the Middle Ages.
questions.evidence: In the European universities of the Middle Ages ... discuss questions ... with people who had made a special study

questions.explanation: The passage places the emergence of the written examination in the nineteenth century, while qualifying this historical claim with 'probably'.
questions.evidence: was probably not known until the nineteenth century

questions.explanation: The passage suggests reasons for written tests but gives no survey or statement about most people's preference in that century.
questions.evidence: Perhaps it came into existence with the great increase in population

questions.explanation: The wrong statements are designed to look like possible answers to students who have not learned the material properly.
questions.evidence: three statements that look like answers to students who have not learned the material properly

questions.explanation: The passage says objective tests can reveal a great deal about a student's knowledge in a short time.
questions.evidence: In a short time, the teacher can find out a great deal

questions.explanation: One stated weakness is that a student may guess correctly without knowing the material.
questions.evidence: A lucky student may guess the correct answer without really knowing the material.

questions.explanation: The passage discusses students' essay-writing abilities, but it does not say good essay writers always prefer that test type.
questions.evidence: Some students are able to write rather good answers

questions.explanation: Some students know the material but still have difficulty expressing their ideas in an essay.
questions.evidence: students who actually know the material have trouble expressing their ideas in essay form

questions.explanation: Combining the two test types is said to give a fairly clear picture of knowledge. The passage does not state that both teachers and students feel quite satisfied with the combination.
questions.evidence: a fairly clear picture of the student's knowledge can usually be obtained
